title: Electrophysiological mapping of the motor cortex in disorders of the corticomotoneuronal and extrapyramidal motor systems
summary:
In this study, both healthy participants and patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are examined. The goal is to better understand how the brain controls simple movements such as those of the tongue, hand, and foot.
For this purpose, brain activity is measured using magnetoencephalography (MEG), a non-invasive method, while participants perform simple, visually instructed movements. At the same time, muscle activity is recorded with electrodes placed on the skin (electromyography, EMG).  In healthy participants, the normal patterns of brain activity during movement are recorded. In patients with Parkinson’s disease, we investigate how deep brain stimulation (DBS) influences these activity patterns. In patients with ALS, movement and brain signals are measured to identify disease-related changes. The study is expected to provide new insights into how the brain controls movement, how neurological diseases affect these processes, and how treatments such as DBS work.
conditions: Spinal muscular atrophy and related syndromes

interventions.name: In this prospective study, we aim at mapping the electrophysiological architecture of the motor cortex using non-invasive Magnetoencephalography (MEG). Brain activity is acquired using MEG during simple movements of tongue, hand, and foot. There will be 30 repetitions (movement executions) per body

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Healthy participants (Study Part 1):
No neurological, psychiatric, or internal medical disorders
Age > 18 years
Right-handed: Edinburgh Handedness Inventory Test
No cognitive impairment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) > 25
No motor deficits: UPDRS III ≥ 1
Capacity to provide informed consent
Understanding of the study procedures and written informed consent to participate

Patients with Parkinson’s disease (Study Parts 2 and 3):
Diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease
Treatment with deep brain stimulation (DBS) using directional electrodes
Either completion of follow-up visits approx. 3 months and 12 months after DBS surgery or consent to participate in follow-up visits approx. 3 months and 12 months after DBS surgery (part of routine clinical care at our center)
Age > 40 years
Capacity to provide informed consent
Understanding of the study procedures and written informed consent to participate

Patients with ALS (Study Part 4):
Age > 18 years
Clinically confirmed diagnosis of ALS according to the Gold Coast criteria
Capacity to provide informed consent
Understanding of the study procedures and written informed consent to participate
Exclusion criteria:
Healthy participants:
Parkinson’s disease or other severe neurological, internal medical, or psychiatric disorders
Reduced cognitive abilities: MoCA < 25
Implants causing significant ferromagnetic artifacts (which would make MEG analysis impossible), such as tattoos containing metal, pacemakers, defibrillators, implanted pumps, and other interfering metallic implants
Large head circumference preventing comfortable positioning within the MEG helmet
Claustrophobia

Patients with Parkinson’s disease:
Additional severe neurological, internal medical, or psychiatric disorders
Reduced cognitive abilities: MoCA < 25
Implants causing significant ferromagnetic artifacts (which would make MEG analysis impossible), such as tattoos containing metal, pacemakers, defibrillators, implanted pumps, and other interfering metallic implants, with the exception of the DBS system
Large head circumference preventing comfortable positioning within the MEG helmet
Claustrophobia

Patients with ALS:
Additional severe neurological, internal medical, or psychiatric disorders
Implants causing significant ferromagnetic artifacts (which would make MEG analysis impossible), such as tattoos containing metal, pacemakers, defibrillators, implanted pumps, and other interfering metallic implants
Large head circumference preventing comfortable positioning within the MEG helmet
Claustrophobia
